opus-5.5.text:
I don't really see it as a strict tradeoff, honestly. I think they're two sides of the same thing, and over time they converge.

If you look at how reasoning developed over the past couple of years, a lot of it came from letting the model think longer, explore different paths, reflect, and correct itself. That's what test-time scaling is, and it's been very powerful, especially for math, coding, and other problems where there's a clear answer you can verify. But it's still a kind of closed loop. The model is talking to itself. Everything it needs is already in the context, and it's just working out the consequences.

Interacting with an environment is different. Now the model takes an action, the world responds, and the response contains information the model didn't have before. Maybe it searches something, runs some code, clicks around in a browser, calls a tool. The feedback can be noisy, it can be delayed, it can be surprising. So the model has to plan over a much longer horizon, deal with uncertainty, and update its beliefs as it goes. In a sense, that's reasoning too, but reasoning that's grounded in real feedback rather than only in its own thoughts.

So the question isn't really "reasoning or agency." It's more about where you put your compute and your training signal. If you only push pure reasoning, you get a model that's very strong at self-contained problems but may be fragile when it has to operate in the real world for many steps. If you only push interaction without strong reasoning, you get an agent that can call tools but doesn't really know what it's doing, so it makes a lot of shallow mistakes and can't recover.

What we've found is that the most interesting gains come when you train them together, using reinforcement learning on long-horizon tasks where the model has to think, act, observe, and think again, maybe hundreds of times. Then the reasoning becomes more useful because it's tied to actual outcomes, and the interaction becomes more intelligent because there's real thinking behind each step.

There are practical tensions, of course. Long thinking costs tokens and latency. Environment interaction is expensive to build and hard to scale. You need good environments and good reward signals, and they're much harder to construct than a math dataset with answers. So at any given moment, a team has to decide what the bottleneck is. But I think in the long run, the ceiling is set by the agentic side. A model that can only think, no matter how deeply, is limited by what's in its head. A model that can think and act can keep acquiring new information and actually get things done. That's where I think the next big leap comes from.

r001.rationale: It describes the model taking an action, receiving the world’s response, and gaining information it did not have before.

r002.rationale: It argues that the strongest gains come from training reasoning and interaction together, and that models need to think and act to reach their potential.

r003.rationale: It mentions practical costs and choosing a development bottleneck, but does not say that a dynamic market makes short-term strategy differences consequential.

fable-5.1.text:
I don't think they're really in tension; I think they're two sides of the same thing, and the order in which you build them matters.

Reasoning is the foundation. If a model can't think carefully over a long horizon, hold a problem in its head, check its own work, and recover when it's wrong, then giving it tools and an environment just lets it make mistakes faster. The agent fails on step three and never notices. So in that sense, reasoning comes first. The "thinking" ability is what makes everything else compound.

But reasoning in isolation has a ceiling. If a model only ever reasons inside its own head, it's reasoning about a static snapshot of the world, and it can't verify anything. Interacting with an environment, calling a tool, running code, searching, getting feedback, is what closes the loop. The environment becomes a source of ground truth and a source of new training signal. So agentic ability is not a separate skill you bolt on; it's reasoning that extends outward, where the "thought" includes an action and the observation that comes back.

Where the real tradeoff shows up is in resources and in data. Long-horizon agent tasks are expensive: the trajectories are long, the rewards are sparse, and you need environments that are realistic enough to matter. Pure reasoning tasks, like math or code, are much cheaper to scale because verification is clean. So the practical question is how much of your compute and RL budget you spend on each. My view is you shouldn't treat them as two buckets. You build the reasoning base, then you design environments where improving at the task requires both thinking deeply and acting well, so the model learns to decide when to think more and when to go look. That meta-skill, knowing when to stop deliberating and interact with the world, is really the thing we care about.

And honestly, the thing that has surprised me is how much agentic training feeds back into reasoning. When a model has to act and then face the consequences, it gets more honest with itself. It learns to doubt its own assumptions. So I'd say: start with reasoning, but don't wait too long to put it in a world.

r001.rationale: The response says acting in an environment and receiving observations closes the loop, providing feedback and new training signal.

r002.rationale: It describes reasoning and environmental interaction as two sides of the same capability, and says reasoning alone has a ceiling.

r003.rationale: The response discusses compute, data, and training tradeoffs, but does not mention a dynamic market or short-term strategic differences becoming consequential.

astra-6.text:
I think reasoning and interacting with an environment are complementary. Reasoning lets a model consider possible actions before taking them, while interaction gives it new information and feedback. The important question is how to allocate effort between the two.

For example, if a model is missing a crucial piece of information, thinking longer may not help. It should take an action, observe the result, and then update its plan. But if an action is costly or difficult to reverse, spending more time reasoning beforehand can be valuable.

So I wouldn’t optimize these capabilities independently. I’d want a model to learn the whole loop: when to think, when to act, and how to revise its reasoning based on what actually happens. Ultimately, the measure is whether it can accomplish the task, not simply how much reasoning it produces.

r001.rationale: It describes acting, observing the result, and updating the plan, identifying interaction as a source of environmental feedback.

r002.rationale: It says reasoning and environmental interaction are complementary and that the model should learn the full think–act–revise loop to accomplish tasks.

r003.rationale: It makes no mention of a dynamic market or short-term differences between AI development strategies.

sol-6.1.text:
I think reasoning and interaction are complementary. Reasoning lets a model do more with each interaction: it can plan, consider different possibilities, and decide what information it needs. But interaction gives it feedback that it can’t get just by thinking longer.

For example, if you’re solving a problem in an unfamiliar environment, you can spend a lot of time reasoning from assumptions that turn out to be wrong. Sometimes the best next step is to take an action, observe the result, and update your understanding. On the other hand, acting without enough reasoning can waste time or lead to mistakes.

So the important capability is deciding when to think and when to act. Ideally, you train them together, so reasoning helps the model interact more effectively, and feedback from the environment helps improve its reasoning.
